extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of history, literary criticism, and moral/philosophical essays
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for recognizing and judging 'great men' / heroes in history and literature — what moral, intellectual, and practical qualities make a man truly great. Focuses on examples (Luther, Knox) to illustrate criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standing on reality (fact, not semblance)
rubrics_metrics.description: A great man restores people to reality by exposing and rejecting mere semblances, forms, or false appearances that have been taken for truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle treats Luther as a 'Prophet Idol-breaker' who told men that 'God's-world stood not on semblances but on realities'; the burning of the Pope's Bull is given as the emblem of rejecting 'Formulism, Pagan Popeism, and other Falsehood and corrupt Semblance.' The criterion emphasizes active repudiation of institutional or ceremonial falsities in favor of factual, living truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adherence to conscience and truth (unwillingness to recant)
rubrics_metrics.description: Refusal to act against one's conscience or to renounce convictions except when convincingly refuted; moral firmness grounded in truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by Luther at the Diet of Worms: 'neither safe nor prudent to do aught against conscience. Here stand I; I can do no other.' Carlyle presents this as central: a hero must hold to what he believes to be sound truth and the Word of God unless decisively overturned by proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courage and valor (combative but principled)
rubrics_metrics.description: A hero can fight and conquer falsehoods — boldness and readiness to confront opposition — but this courage is principled, not mere ferocity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle praises Luther as 'a right piece of human Valor' whose defiance (e.g., at Worms, against 'Devils') proves fearlessness. He warns against confusing courage with brutal ferocity: heroism must combine boldness with thought, affection, and restraint (the tiger is fierce but not heroic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Discernment and leadership (planting oneself where truth lies)
rubrics_metrics.description: The capacity to discern the true heart of a matter and to plant oneself firmly there so others can rally; a kingly faculty of judgment and initiative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle notes that to continue as a leader one 'must have the gift to discern at all turns where the true heart of the matter lies, and to plant himself courageously on that, as a strong true man, that other true men may rally round him there.' This combines judgment, courage, and presence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genuine tolerance (distinguish essentials from nonessentials)
rubrics_metrics.description: A healthy tolerance that allows nonessential differences to persist while reserving judgment for essential matters of truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: when criticized for allowing a preacher to wear a cassock, Luther answers 'Let him have a cassock to preach in; let him have three cassocks if he find benefit in them!' Carlyle calls this a 'very genuine kind of tolerance' — tolerance of forms that do not threaten core truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Righteous intolerance (resisting and extinguishing falsehood)
rubrics_metrics.description: When confronted with falsehood that undermines truth or harms souls, a hero must actively resist rather than passively tolerate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle insists 'we are here to resist, to control and vanquish' falsehoods; Knox's flinging of the painted image ('a pented bredd') into the river exemplifies refusing to worship apparent falsehood. Tolerance has limits when essentials are at stake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity and truthfulness (primary characteristic of a hero)
rubrics_metrics.description: Uncompromising sincerity — clinging to reality and truth — is the fundamental trait that makes an individual heroic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle explicitly states the 'primary characteristic of a Hero, that he is sincere,' using Knox as the exemplar: 'He lies there who never feared the face of man.' Sincerity is shown by steadfastness under pressure and unwillingness to feign belief or compromise core convictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compassionate heart (gentleness, pity, love)
rubrics_metrics.description: True courage coexists with gentleness, pity, and affectionate feeling; the heroic heart is tender as well as brave.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle stresses Luther's tenderness — his behavior at his daughter's death, love of music, and 'soft breathings of affection.' Courage without pity is inferior; the genuinely valiant person is also capable of deep feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral endurance and willingness to suffer
rubrics_metrics.description: A hero endures hardship, persecution, exile, or bodily suffering for the cause; readiness for sacrifice is evidence of authenticity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knox's history (galley-slave, exile, persecution) is cited as proof: 'A man sent to row in French Galleys... cannot always be in the mildest humor!' Endurance and suffering—but not self-seeking—validate commitment to principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stability and stewardship (remaining to guide the movement)
rubrics_metrics.description: A hero's staying power — remaining alive and central to steer a movement — prevents chaos and moderates revolution; the ability to hold the center matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle notes that great wars and disunion began after Luther's death and praises that 'none of them began so long as he continued living.' The leader who can maintain influence can keep a revolution more ordered and constructive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical emphasis and pursuit of Order grounded in Truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Heroes seek practical, truth-based order rather than false peace or inert conformity; they aim to put right what is false and restore genuine social or spiritual order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle contrasts 'a brutal lethargy' (dead peace) with 'a living peace' and says 'Order is Truth' — a hero works to 'extinguish Falsehoods, and put an end to them' so that order may be genuine, not mere semblance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor, sociability, and human wholesomeness
rubrics_metrics.description: A complete heroic nature includes social warmth, humor, and fellow-feeling; the hero is brother to high and low.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle attributes to Knox a 'vein of drollery' and a 'cheery social man' persona; Luther's table-talk and love of music are also examples. These qualities humanize heroes and make them beloved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary and intellectual force (clear expression that moves others)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capacity to express ideas in powerful, idiomatic, and influential language that can galvanize others and shape cultural life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Luther's writings are praised for 'a rugged honesty, homeliness, simplicity' and idiomatic power; Carlyle notes his dialect 'became the language of all writing.' The hero's words can be 'half-battles' — rhetorically formative and mobilizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emergent, non-ambitious vocation (called rather than self-seeking)
rubrics_metrics.description: True heroes often do not seek power or position; they answer a call or are thrust into leadership by circumstances and conviction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle recounts Knox's reluctant emergence (bursting into tears when called to speak) and emphasizes that Knox's prophetic role 'was not of his seeking.' The absence of personal ambition is a mark of authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity to form collective belief ('nation of heroes')
rubrics_metrics.description: Heroes can inspire communal faith and a moral-political reformation that shapes a people (e.g., Puritanism producing a 'believing nation').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle argues Puritanism in England and Scotland became 'a real business of the heart' and produced lasting institutional and cultural fruits (Scotch literature, American settlements). The hero's influence is measured by the depth and durability of the faith or civic character he kindles.
